claims.text: Enhanced initial short-range chemical ordering increases resistance to phase segregation relative to a random chemical arrangement.
Enhanced initial short-range chemical ordering increases oxidation resistance relative to a random chemical arrangement.
The improved stability produced by enhanced short-range order is entropy-driven.
Low-noble-metal, near-equiatomic CoNiCuZn-based nanoparticles can form a solid solution with tunable short-range chemical order.
Synthesis conditions can be controlled to produce otherwise comparable nanoparticles with enhanced versus relatively random short-range chemical order.
Local chemical ordering maintains atomic-scale compositional homogeneity.
Local chemical ordering suppresses nucleation of segregated phases.
High configurational entropy can favor a uniform multielement solid solution over intermetallic formation or phase segregation.
Entropy-driven stabilization counteracts thermally activated diffusion and elemental segregation.
Enhanced short-range order raises the energy barrier for phase separation.
Enhanced short-range order raises the energy barrier for oxidation.
Enhanced-order nanoparticles will retain a single-phase structure with fewer segregated domains after high-temperature exposure.
Enhanced-order nanoparticles will exhibit less oxidation than randomly ordered nanoparticles under identical reactive high-temperature conditions.
Randomly arranged baseline nanoparticles have a greater tendency toward phase separation under reactive high-temperature exposure.
Randomly arranged baseline nanoparticles have a greater tendency toward oxidation under reactive high-temperature exposure.
The proposed hypothesis is restricted to low-noble-metal multielement nanoparticles tested at 773–1173 K in reactive environments.
The result may not extrapolate to substantially different compositions, synthesis methods, or temperature ranges.
The magnitude of stabilization and the contributions of kinetic barriers and surface oxidation are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes the ordered sample's superior stability to entropy-driven stabilization, but the relatively random baseline ordinarily has greater configurational entropy. No separate enthalpic or kinetic argument is supplied to reconcile enhanced ordering with an entropy-based advantage over the random state.
